8.t: MAY-LOWER SIX
Spring, printemps, Friithling, in wharever language it js. still the most romantic of seasons，
and for an 18 year old, it can but promise all the aspirations and warmth radiated in Botricelli's
Primavera.
The velvety mist of the Chanps Elysees gently dissolving into the dawn of the first
morning in Spring, or the splendours of a Venerian Iwilight reflecred in the Adriatic in late
Spring is a sight thar men would gladly have seen and died, but for me there would be no
place more beaurifil than our avente - all 349 paces of it! Be it in Spring. Summer, Autumn，
or Winter, I shall always find it most enchanting, but especially in Spring, not so much Decause
tien, the Bauhinias orchestrated in full blossom with the delicacy depicted only in fairytales and
enhanced Oy sweet-scented fowers springing into exristence like the vivacious phrases of Strauss*
Till Eulenpiegel is something Which transcends the soul more than feasts the eyes, as because
this is the way that I shall last.see il and forever remember it.
More and more lovely does the avenue grow each day as the Summer holidays approach.
However, for the first time, I cannot regard it so much as the approach of the holidays as the
ending of the school year, the cumination of the eternal present Where the meaning of tne
past is decided and the furure formed, and now all thar remains is for me to conclude six of
the most unforgettable years in one month.
May shall pass as quickly as Lower Six.
and
this is the way I want it to be, just as if I could relive my whole life I would nor change a thing.
I might never have realised that I was in Form Six had I not been given the chance of
helping one of the Form I classes with their play.In addition to giving me sore throat and
an opportunity of testing my patience to beyond its limits, those darling little “angels' gave me
the most marvellous present ever possible, the chance of reliving the past six years, each of
which with its own particular Character, expectations and anxieties, and Lower Six is but a
fartastically superfuous and incongruous amassment of them all. Within the few all too short
month of this wonderful year, our education has been crowned a touch of Tolstoy, Freua，
Fournier, Picasso, Tchaikovsky, Camus, Fromm, Debussy, Machiavelli, Van Gogh, Jesus Christ
Superstar, Marx, de Cervantes, von Goethe, Chekhov, Ionesco and last but not least, Walt Disney
（all very high sounding, none of which we even pretended to comprehend except perhaps the
last）.
It is said that the best time to leave a thing is at its prime, however this is one time
where I neither have the wish nor the ability to be so rational.
Now suddenly things so minute
become such a memorable pert of my education, things Like the smell of beef being fried drift-
ing up from the kirchen just before lunch, going to the canteen to get the coupons for Lunch，
the noise of the cicadas that makes listening to the teacher virtually impossible, the singing of
the birds in the chapel which makes lite so beautiful, the scent of the flowers along the avenue
Friends made during school days are the best friends, for at this time of our lives, our
need to understand and be wnderstood is greatest.
However, when we are half the world apart
one does wonder whether it would be hoping against hope that we do not change, and even
if that be possible, we still mature and grow up.
The past remains in the past and is only Te-
called to memory as a sweet Lingering fragrance of melancholy.
Much be it my most profound desire to bring forth a finale to equal the momentum of
that of the Choral Symphony or the elegance of that of A Tale of Iwo Ciries, I can but think
of one thing
Adios mis amigos，
Adien our Wah Yan, Adiet.
Anthony Choy

16.t: Mr. FRANCIS NG LUT WAI
Francis Ng had almost reached 60 when he died in August 1973. As a boy he
was at school in St. Joseph's College and later in La Salle. He did teacher training and
was invited by Brother Aimar to teach in La Salle College, Boundary Street. During
the Japanese occupation. after a short interlude working on ships, Francis found it
expedient to leave Hong Kong and go back to the family village near Nam Hoi. There，
he and his wife conducted a school for the village children. Soon after the end of the
Pacific War, he made his way back to Hong Kong and joined the staff of Wah Yan at
Robinson Rd. As a teacher he was quiet, steady and hardworking. In 1951 he became
ill with cancer of the throat. Fortunately, the disease responded well to deep X-ray
treatment and he was able to teach without difliculty. There was no recurrence until
June 1973 when he began to feel unwell. The doctors did everything possible, but had
to admit that he had only a month to live. He took the verdict calmly and set about
preparing for death. He said more than once that he was thankful to God that he had
not died in 1951 when his children were small but that he was able to live to see them
grown up and able to make their way in the world. He was grateful too that his
children were so good and loving towards their parents. He was greatly consoled dur-
ing those last days that his wife and children were all the time in attendance at his
bedside.
Francis has lett his family and all of us the example of a good lite which is more
precious than gold.

the certificates and prizes.
Atter the presentation and the

his speech. Firstly, he gave us some ideas on his school life in Wah Yan. Then
he gave his ideas on
the education system in Hong Kong which he ended with
these words;For his education to be complete, the child must not only be led to self-
realisation, to the control of natural primitive impulses for the good of the whole, bu！
he should learn also, both at home and at school, that physical well-being and material
possesslons are not the whole of life: they are essential only as a basis for it. He should
learn that the creations of man's mind and spirit are also 1mportant, that they are, In
fact, the source of some of man's deepest satisfactions. He should therefore be given

should be opened to him, so that he may have throughout his life a source of mental
and spiritual refreshment.
Most people today recognise the importance of giving the
child a healthy body and of providing him with all those things that give him the
foundations of physical health.
Unfortunately, they do not realise with anything like
the same Clarty that It Is equally important for him to have those things that lead to

35.t: School Students' Seminar
The Seminar was conducted through 4 steps: lectures, panel discussions，
group discussions, and plenary sessions. We had lectures and discussions on：
1. the general values of extra-curricular activities on education as a
whole.
2. the value of extra-curricular activities in the acquirement of knowledge.
3. the value of extra-curricular activities in the recreational aspect.
4. the value of extra-curricular activities in the constructive aspect.
Ihe conclusions discussions showed that extra-curricular activities is
getting more and more attention and that students are becoming more active
in this respect. There were certain problems however hailed as obstacles to
the development of extra-curricular activities. Among them, finance, facilities，
full support from students and authorities, awareness among students, etc.
There were, of course, suggested remedies to any question raised and all the
materials of the discussions were published in April in the form of a Report
which was prepared by the organising committee and sent to delegates, schools，
government departments, organisations concerned, etc.
When requested to voice their opinions and views during the overall
conclusion and review of the Seminar, most of the groups said that the
delegates felt the Seminar was quite an experience, that they have learned
something from the lectures and discussions and also that the organising
committee was efficient.
Speaking from the standpoint of the organiser they truly feel that even if
not much results from what they have found out during the Seminar, there is
one thing they have truly experienced-community spirit. The organisers and
delegates alike were co-operative, enthusiastic, gay and above all friendly.
Before running off the report, the committee would like to take this oppor-
tunity to thank once again, Mr. Canning for being the patron, the Central
District Officers, Mrs. O. Rahmin and Mr. Leung Kwong Hung for their
sponsoring the project.
They also grateful to all the advisers for their
guidance and last, but not least, the delegates for their cooperation and con-
tribution. They wish the next.seminar would be even more successful.

other similar function is carried out, such defects will be corrected and the whole pro-

others played games of majong, poker and even the traditional Chinese bridge.

76.t: TEE DISTAALATTON OP MGR PSUSR W.S HEE AS BISEOP
Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception, April, 20, 1974.
BISHOP LEP'S SERMON
My dear Brothers and Sisters in Cfarist，
A year ago we Lost our beloved Bishop Francis Hsu.
I have now been called to succeea him to the Diocese of Hong Kong•
To be Bishop of Hong Kong is a great responsibility which becomes
awsome when it involves succeeding two Bishops whom so many of us
remember and Loved so much - Bishop Bianchi and Bishop Hsu - two
Bishops of different talents but each of whom gave so much.
It has not been easy for me to accept, and face up to, this responsibility; it
would be too much for me were it not that I can call upon so much help
help from God and help from my collaborators, the priests and religious working
with me in this Diocese, and from the faithful whom we serve.
All this is a source
To God I pray, especially at this my Installation ceremony, that he will give me the
strength to support my weakness unworthy though I am.
Without Him my work wil
be in vain.
To all the priests and religious working with me in Hong Kong of whatever origin
and Whatever nationality / give special thanks for their support and Joyalty during the past
year and 1 am confdent I can count on their continued
Co-operation during the coming
years.
In this cosmopolitan society of Hong Kong, at the beginning of this our plurai age，
and in these material times, we need that strong spiritual leadership which can only come
from a firm unity of all the various talents and experiences which we find today among the
clergy and religious here - a unity which can only grow out of a selfess enthusiasm for
spreading and establishing the word of God in the hearts of the Faithful: and out of a
Drotherly love founded on that personal sacrifice to which priests and religious are dedicated
a brothery Love Which involves deep Charity and care and consideration for others，
irrespective of age, race and outlook - a brotherly
love which involves giving more than
receiving.
To all our Faithful and to those of our friends not of our Fold I express my apprecia-
tion and grattude for the support and Loyalty you give to our Diocese.
Your good will and
sincerity are my encouragement to take up the appointment to which I have been called.
All these matters give me the assurance and confidence to accept this appointment and
t0 make my Pleage to the Holy See.
Today, in the presence of Archbishop Simon Lourdusamy, Secretary of the Sacred
Congregation for the Evangelization of Peoples and of you all, I make my pledge of Joyalty
again to the Vicar of Christ, our Holy Father. I sincerely wish that he, as successor of Peter，
who had been entrusted by Our Lord with the task of strengthening his brethren, will
strengthen me, the least of his brethren！
The Bishop, as a father, should be ready to show love and concern to each and every
one; and, as a Pastor, should be prepared to Lead his fock to Christ. Such a father and
pastor, I wish to be. The Good Shepherd is always ready to give all of himself for his
flock, and I wish to be such a Shepherd.
But to be all of this I need your prayers and
God's grace.
Let us all now go forward in unity to promote God's Kingdom, a Kingdom of truth
and life, of holiness and grace, of justice, Love and peace.
May almignty God bless us alll

One Sunday morning we were to set off to Shek-O for a picnic. Unfortunately，
just when we were ready, we found dark clouds in the sky. In the next second it began
to rain heavily. How we missed the nice swim we might have！
We were disappointed and looked gloomily out of the windows. People without
raincoats or umbrellas were running. Some covered their heads with newspapers and
others ran until they got shelter. The unfortunate ones were badly splashed by cars.
Most buses, trams and taxi-cabs were full. There were shelters too. What we saw made
us laugh and forget our disappointment.

6B1 Andrew Peng
Lis a big, day school in Wanchai and is run by Jesuit Fathers and the Pun U
Issociation. Altogether there are twelve Classrooms and Since It Is Dl-sesslonal, thero
are twenty-four classes.
The big pitch, the hall and the billiard room are the places where we have
plenty of fun for our games including basketball, football, biliards, chess, aeroplanes，
paper-balls and even monkey games. The last three games must appear strange to many，
but do come and see how we play them and how happy we are. During recess time，
our Headmaster, Rev. Fr. Mallin, and some other teachers are often with us.
We have a library on the third floor and it has a collection of over a thousand
books. The movie-room is also on the third floor. Once a week we are audience of
selected films. The tuck-shop is small, but it satisfies our needs.
I am in the morning session and like most other pupils I go to school by school
bus. School begins at ten to eight, and we have seven periods and two breaks before we
go home for lunch.
Our school supervisor is Rev. Fr. Barrett and our headmaster is Rev. Fr. Mallin.
Rev. Fr. Barrett is also headmaster of Wah Yan College and I think that it is why we
have a good chance of getting into Wah Yan if we succeed in the SSEE.
We respect our teachers and it is our duty to study hard so that our teachers wil
not be disappointed.
